media_strategy.selection_principle: Use all five channels (chart, image, video, audio, interactive_or_map) but anchor every choice in the dataset's actual properties — coordinates → real map; massive heavy-tailed numeric column → sonification; iconic real photographs from Detective → reused rather than generated; one strong still → image2video for the kinetic edge.

chart.reason: The dataset is fundamentally quantitative — Fell/Found splits, mass distributions, decade trends, family compositions. Charts are how those land.

image.reason: The Detective downloaded 7 real Wikimedia photographs of the named flagship meteorites. They are credible, specific, and visually striking — far stronger than any generated stand-in. We reuse them as section anchors rather than generate.

video.reason: We have one iconic still (Hoba). image2video animates it as the teaser, adding kinetic life without losing the credibility of a real Namibian photo.

audio.reason: The top-20 mass column is a small ranked sequence — exactly what sonification handles well. Mapping log(mass) to pitch turns the descending bar chart into a one-bar melody readers can hear while watching the bars highlight. Paired with the chart, click-to-play, never autoplay.

interactive_or_map.reason: 84% of rows have lat/long; an interactive Leaflet map of Fells (red) over Founds (blue sample) is the centrepiece and the only way the Antarctic + desert pattern lands physically. A separate guess-first quiz in edt_01 gives the hook a participatory moment.

des_01.label: Teaser hero — Hoba meteorite still (real Wikimedia photo)

content.license: CC BY 2.0 — Eugen Zibiso via Wikimedia Commons

des_01.brief: Full-bleed hero image at the top of the page: the 60-ton Hoba iron meteorite resting in its Namibian open-air amphitheatre. Mood: weight, stillness, eighty thousand years sitting in one place. Caption underneath credits CC BY 2.0 Eugen Zibiso.
des_01.rationale: The single heaviest row in the dataset is also the single most photographable object. Using a real photo of the named heavyweight from row 1 is more credible and more grounded than any generated cinematic.

des_02.label: Teaser motion — image2video parallax push-in on Hoba

content.prompt: very slow cinematic parallax push-in toward the giant iron Hoba meteorite resting in its open-air stone amphitheatre in Namibia; soft warm afternoon light, no people in frame, no camera shake, ambient dust catching the light

des_02.brief: Six-second clip generated from the Hoba still — slow parallax push-in. Plays muted, looped, behind the hero headline. Plain still (des_01) is the no-JS fallback.
des_02.rationale: Image2video preserves the credibility of the real photograph while giving the teaser the kinetic edge a pure still cannot.

des_03.label: Big stat callout — 2.42% Fell

content.label: of the 45,716 named meteorites in the catalogue were ever observed falling. 1,107 of them. The other 44,609 were found later.

des_03.brief: Oversized 88px stat number with a 16px-line eyebrow above it ('OBSERVED FALLS') and a one-sentence caption below. Sits to the left of the body text at the top of edt_01. Pure typographic moment — no chart bars or icons.
des_03.rationale: The hook deserves a single number with no decoration. Anything more — a chart, a donut — softens the punch.

des_04.label: Guess-first quiz — How many were seen falling?

content.initial_state: Reader sees a card with the prompt: 'Of the 45,716 named meteorites in this catalogue, what fraction were ever observed falling?' and four buttons: 1 in 5, 1 in 10, 1 in 20, 1 in 50.
content.transition: Selected button flips to highlighted, a small horizontal bar grows from 0 to 100% showing the picked value; then the actual value (1 in 41) animates in as a second darker bar with a tooltip showing 1,107 / 45,716.
content.payoff: Reader sees their guess vs reality side by side. Caption reveals the true rate is roughly one fall observed every two months across the entire planet.

des_04.brief: A small four-option quiz that lets the reader commit a guess before the 2.42% number is unveiled. Sits just after des_03's stat callout so readers who skim get the answer; readers who engage get the surprise.
des_04.rationale: The finding is genuinely surprising and a guess-first interaction multiplies the impact for engaged readers. Non-interactive readers still see the stat callout.

des_05.label: Decade stacked-bar chart — Fell vs Found 1700-2010

content.interaction: hover tooltip with decade, Fell count, Found count, Total; the 1970 bar gets a fixed annotation arrow

des_05.brief: Stacked-bar chart, decade on x, count on y. Fell in muted red on the bottom of each stack, Found in a saturated blue on top. The Fell stripe stays flat-ish at 50-90/decade; the Found stripe is invisible until the 1880s, then explodes after 1960. A static annotation arrow pinpoints the 1970 decade.
des_05.rationale: The whole point of this section is the visual shape — Fell flat, Found exploding. Stacked bars make both stories readable in one image.

des_06.label: Antarctic recovery — real photo
des_06.brief: Half-width image right of the decade chart caption — a researcher on Antarctic ice with a meteorite. Tight crop, no logos. Sells the operational reality behind the 1970s spike.
des_06.rationale: Pairs the chart's abstract spike with the physical reality. Reusing a NASA photo is more credible than a generated illustration.

des_07.label: Centrepiece interactive map — Fells (red) over Founds (blue)

content.initial_state: Full-width world map at zoom ~1.5, dark editorial basemap. All 1,107 Fells render as 5px red circles; 2,000 sampled Founds as 2px light-blue dots underneath. The Antarctic ice and three desert belts (Sahara, Arabia, Atacama) appear as natural clusters of blue.
content.trigger: Hover a marker → tooltip with name, year, mass (kg), recclass, fall type. Click a marker → bottom-left detail panel pins that meteorite. Zoom in to see individual Antarctic blue-ice fields resolve.
content.transition: A small top-right legend explains red = observed Fell, blue = later Find. A toggle button lets the reader hide Founds (Fells-only mode) to reveal how scattered observed falls are vs how concentrated Finds are.
content.payoff: Reader can physically see the two patterns: red dots are roughly where humans live and notice things (Europe, India, eastern US, Japan); blue dots cluster in the cold and the dry. The two are barely overlapping.

des_07.brief: The page's centerpiece. ~600px tall. Two layers — Fells (red, all 1,097 geocoded ones) and a 2,000-Found sample (light blue). Toggle to hide Founds. Click markers for details. The visual sells the editorial argument in 1 second.
des_07.rationale: The dataset has lat/long; this is the canonical use case for an interactive map and the section's editorial brief explicitly asks for one.

des_08.label: Log-bucket mass histogram

content.interaction: hover tooltip with exact count; the bucket containing Hoba (10-100t) gets a tiny label '60-ton Hoba lives here'

des_08.brief: Horizontal bar chart, one bar per log decade of mass. Bar lengths show row counts. The 10-100 g bar is the giant; everything to its right dwindles to slivers. Static annotation arrows mark median location and the Hoba bucket.
des_08.rationale: Log-scale histograms read best horizontally; the 9 buckets fit cleanly stacked. Static is fine — no exploration adds anything.

des_09.label: Top 20 heaviest — leaderboard with sonification

content.highlight_rule: label each bar with mass in tonnes and (rank-19) Jilin H5 gets a callout 'first non-iron'
content.interaction: hover tooltip with name, mass (kg + tonnes), recclass, fall, year, country (from lat/lon); click highlights the row in the sonification (des_10)

des_09.brief: Vertical leaderboard, top to bottom: Hoba, Cape York, Campo del Cielo, Canyon Diablo, Armanty ... Jilin. Bars coloured by family — the wall of brown irons is instantly visible. The Jilin bar at rank 19 is the only blue and gets the only annotation: 'first non-iron'.
des_09.rationale: The story is 'wall of iron'; coloring by family forces that pattern to the foreground. Log scale prevents Hoba's 60,000 kg from crushing the lower rows visually.

des_10.label: Sonification — top 20 mass as 20-note marimba sequence

content.why_audio: The top-20 mass column is a small monotone-decreasing sequence over three orders of magnitude. Mapping log(mass) to pitch turns the chart's bars into a melody — readers hear how steeply the catalogue drops from Hoba (60 t) to Vaca Muerta (3.8 t). Adds a sensory channel for the tail.
content.trigger: Click 'Play the leaderboard' button under the chart in des_09. Never autoplay.
content.ui_form: chart-synced sonification — each bar in des_09 briefly highlights as its tone plays; current name labelled below the play button.

content.prompt: 20 short marimba notes, one per beat, sonification of meteorite masses from largest to smallest: starts on a low resonant bass note (60 tonne Hoba) and steps gradually up the scale in proportion to log-mass — the descending size becomes an ascending pitch line, finishing on a bright high note. No reverb, dry intimate close-miked marimba, 90 BPM, no melody beyond the data progression, no vocals, 8 seconds total

content.fallback: If audio is muted or unsupported, the chart alone communicates the leaderboard; the play button is disabled with a tooltip.
content.novelty_note: Not the generic 'audio card with waveform bars' pattern — this audio is tied to a specific chart's bars and only valuable while watching them highlight.

des_10.brief: An eight-second marimba sequence that walks the top-20 leaderboard from heaviest to lightest. Each tone is timed so the bar in des_09 lights up beneath it. Sits as a single play button under the leaderboard chart.
des_10.rationale: Sonification is the data-driven audio fit for a small ranked sequence. The dataset has no obvious sonic dimension otherwise; this is the choice that adds explanation rather than decoration.

des_11.label: Cape York's Ahnighito at AMNH — real photo

content.license: CC BY 2.0 — Mike Cassano via Wikimedia Commons

des_11.brief: Three-column-wide image to the right of the iron-wall paragraph in edt_05. The Ahnighito fragment of Cape York at the American Museum of Natural History — a 34-ton iron block on a steel plinth that goes down to the bedrock. Caption: 'Ahnighito — second-row entry in the catalogue, largest meteorite on public museum display anywhere.'
des_11.rationale: Hoba is the teaser image; Ahnighito is the proof point for the iron wall. Using two different real museum specimens gives the section breadth.

des_12.label: Twin chart — family by count vs family by median mass

content.highlight_rule: Both panels label Ordinary chondrite (top by count) and Iron meteorite (top by mass) so the flip is obvious
content.interaction: synchronised highlight — hovering a family in either panel highlights it in both

des_12.brief: Two horizontal bar charts side by side. Left: families ranked by count (Ordinary chondrite alone fills 87% of the bar). Right: same families ranked by median mass on log scale (Iron meteorite tops out at 10,000g). Hovering any family highlights it in both panels — the rank-flip is then a single eye movement.
des_12.rationale: The point of this section is that the same set of categories has two opposite rankings. A twin chart with synchronised highlighting makes that flip the entire visual.

des_13.label: Antarctic share by decade — area chart

content.highlight_rule: annotate the 1980 peak ('93% Antarctic') and the 2000s ('hot-desert programs catch up')
content.interaction: hover tooltip with decade, Antarctica count, RestOfWorld count, Antarctica share %

des_13.brief: Stacked area chart, decade on x, geocoded count on y. Antarctica in icy blue at the bottom, rest of world in warm rust on top. Two annotations: 1980 (Antarctica dominates) and 2000 (deserts catch up).
des_13.rationale: An area chart shows the share AND the absolute size simultaneously, which is what this closer needs.

des_14.label: Meteor Crater aerial — real photo close
des_14.brief: Full-width aerial photograph of Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater) in Arizona at the very end of the page. Caption: 'Meteor Crater — the only entry in this catalogue you can still see from orbit. Made by Canyon Diablo, row 4 by mass.'
des_14.rationale: Ends the piece on the largest scale visible: a 1.2 km crater. Ties row 4 of the leaderboard to a feature that is still there in the landscape, fifty thousand years after impact.

page_rhythm.tone: dark editorial, near-monochrome with a single warm accent (the iron-brown used for irons in the leaderboard and the rust used in the closer)
page_rhythm.text_visual_pattern: visual-first hero + alternating text and visual, with the map as the unambiguous centerpiece in the middle of the page
page_rhythm.anti_sameness_notes: No chart streak — every two charts is broken up by either a real photograph (des_06, des_11, des_14) or the central map (des_07). The audio is bound to the leaderboard, not a free-floating tone card. The video is image2video on a real photo, not a generated synthetic.
page_rhythm.typography_notes: Hero stat (des_03) at 88px; section headlines at 32px with a hairline rule; pull quotes (if any) in 18px italic serif. The map (des_07) gets a 24px section heading and breaks out of the body column to full width.
